summary: Sirach 37 begins by warning that not every person called a friend is loyal when trouble comes. It then turns to counsel: some advisers serve their own interests, so the learner must seek trustworthy company, attend to conscience and reason, and ask the Most High for direction. The chapter ends by contrasting empty cleverness with useful wisdom, then gives practical counsel about self-testing and restraint in eating.
whyItMatters: This chapter gathers several of Sirach’s ordinary-life concerns into one place: friendship, advice, speech, wisdom, and appetite. It shows the book’s pattern of joining reverence for God with disciplined judgment in daily relationships.

context.author: Yeshua son of Eleazar son of Sira, a Jerusalem teacher and scribe; his unnamed grandson later translated the Hebrew work into Greek in Egypt.
context.audience: Students seeking disciplined wisdom in Jerusalem, and later Greek-reading Jews who wanted instruction shaped by Israel’s law.
context.date: The Hebrew work was composed in the early second century BC and was likely complete around 180–175 BC. The grandson arrived in Egypt around 132 BC and translated it during his stay.
context.setting: Jerusalem under Hellenistic rule, with temple worship, scribal learning, and ordinary social life taking place within a Greek-speaking Mediterranean world.
context.literaryForm: Wisdom instruction using compact sayings, contrasts, direct address, and practical moral teaching.

outline.heading: Friends in name and friends in trouble
outline.note: The chapter opens by distinguishing real friendship from companionship that fails or turns hostile when affliction comes.

outline.heading: Counsel shaped by self-interest
outline.note: The teacher warns that counselors may advise for their own benefit and lists situations where bias makes advice unreliable.

outline.heading: Trustworthy guidance
outline.note: The learner is urged to stay near a godly person, heed the counsel of the heart, and ask the Most High for direction.

outline.heading: Reason, speech, and wisdom
outline.note: Reason should come before action, the tongue is powerful, and true wisdom benefits both the wise person and the wider people.

outline.heading: Testing desire and restraining appetite
outline.note: The chapter closes with direct address about examining the soul, avoiding harmful indulgence, and taking heed.

keyVerses.text: Every counselor extols counsel, but some give counsel in their own interest.
keyVerses.why: This sentence states the central caution of the chapter’s advice section: counsel must be weighed because advisers may have motives of their own.

keyVerses.text: But rather be continually with a godly man, whom you know to be a keeper of the commandments, who in his soul is as your own soul, and who will grieve with you, if you fail.
keyVerses.why: This verse gives the positive alternative to biased counsel: a trusted companion whose character and loyalty are already known.

keyVerses.text: Above all this ask the Most High that he may direct your way in truth.
keyVerses.why: After discussing friends, counselors, conscience, and watchfulness, the chapter places prayer to the Most High above the other forms of guidance.

keyVerses.text: My son, test your soul in your life. See what is evil for it, and don’t give in to it.
keyVerses.why: This verse begins the closing practical instruction, moving from advice about others to self-examination and restraint.

questions.question: Why does the chapter begin by saying every friend claims to be a friend?
questions.answer: The opening verses warn that the word “friend” can be used loosely. Some companions remain only friends “in name,” while others turn against a person in affliction. The chapter asks readers to judge friendship by loyalty under strain, not by labels.

questions.question: What is the “wicked imagination” in verse 3?
questions.answer: The chapter addresses “wicked imagination” as though this deceitful impulse could answer why it was created and why it covers the land with deception. The surrounding sayings concern false friendship and betrayal. This personified address gives force to the warning about concealed intentions; it does not offer a technical account of how evil originated.

questions.question: Is Sirach saying never to ask advice?
questions.answer: No. The chapter warns against careless dependence on advice from people whose interests are tangled with the decision. It also recommends staying close to a godly person, making the counsel of the heart stand, using reason, and asking the Most High for direction.

questions.question: What does “counsel” mean here?
questions.answer: “Counsel” means advice or guidance about what to do. The chapter uses the word for advice offered by others, the inward counsel of the heart, and the planning that should go before action. Its concern is not advice in general, but advice tested for character, bias, and truth.

questions.question: Why does verse 11 list so many kinds of people not to consult?
questions.answer: The examples show how self-interest or lack of fitness can distort advice. A rival, coward, merchant, buyer, envious person, sluggard, hireling, or idle servant may not be able to counsel fairly in the listed situation. The point is to recognize bias before handing someone influence over a decision.

questions.question: What is the place of the “heart” in this chapter?
questions.answer: Verse 13 says to make “the counsel of your heart stand,” and verse 17 speaks of “the changing of the heart.” In this chapter the heart is connected with inner judgment and the movement from intention to speech and action. It is not treated as enough by itself, since verse 15 says above all to ask the Most High for direction.

questions.question: Why does the chapter say the tongue rules over life and death?
questions.answer: Verses 17-18 connect the changing of the heart with four outcomes: good and evil, life and death. The tongue is named as what continually rules over them. The chapter does not give examples here, but within its flow the saying fits the concern for counsel, speech, and wisdom that either helps or harms.

questions.question: How can someone instruct many and still be unprofitable to his own soul?
questions.answer: Verses 19-21 describe a person who may be clever or subtle in words but lacks wisdom that benefits his own life. The chapter contrasts this with a wise person whose understanding bears trustworthy fruit. It separates verbal skill from wisdom that forms character and serves a community.

questions.question: Why does the chapter end with eating and gluttony?
questions.answer: The final verses move from testing advice to testing the self. Appetite is one concrete place where a person can “see what is evil” and refuse to give in to it. The warning about overeating and gluttony is practical instruction about restraint, not a full medical theory.

glossary.def: A person claimed as a companion; the chapter distinguishes a true friend from someone who is only a friend in name or fails in affliction.
Advice or guidance about what to do; the chapter urges readers to test counsel for hidden interest and to let it go before action.
A title for God in verse 15, where the learner is told to ask that he direct the way in truth.
The organ of speech, used here for the power of words to shape good and evil, life and death.
